limits.text: **Sources.** The source of a track must be yours, in the public domain, or under a licence that allows a derived work (a MIDI of a 19th-century piece is fine; a film theme is not).

rows.heading: Fewer orders: the partial-order reduction (historical, v2.3)

limits.text: **Never use the partial-order reduction to certify that a game has no softlock.** Measured in proof mode in 3.3, it

`--por` only applies to witness searches: in proof mode the solver ignores it and says so.

The solver already merges the states (one hash); what it still paid was the orders in between: k independent pickups before a door are 2^k states when the search cannot finish (a proof of a dead end, a truncated run).
| `tests/fixtures/por.ts`, k pickups then a door that cannot open | states | engine runs |

rows.heading: v3.1: schema 3 and the exhaustive proof (4 October 2026)

limits.text: | solve, whole game, `--prove` | **truncated** at 50 000 states after 408 s, 119 411 runs | not attempted |
The witness did not move between v2.3 and v3.1 (same states, same runs: the stable ids change nothing for the search).

The exhaustive proof is another matter: it visits every reachable state, the partial-order reduction is off in that mode (a reduction must not drop a losing branch from a proof until it has its own equivalence proof), and a 40-room game already exceeds a 50 000-state budget.

rows.heading: v3.2: softlock causes, the proof by chapters, and where the proof stops (4 October 2026)

limits.text: A proof now reports **every** reachable softlock state (`softlockCount`), grouped by the step that lost the game (`softlockCauses`: the first action from a state that could still win into one that cannot), and a proof from "New game" branches over the intro's choices too (the demo's proof grew from 2 176 to 6 528 states: it had only proved the default answer).
One state budget covers the whole proof (`maxStates × 10`, at most 1 000 boundary starts per chapter): past it the result is `truncated`, never green.

**This is a limit of the explicit search as written, not of the engine**: the state keeps every character's exact room and the active character, and a switch of character is a transition of its own, so equivalent states are explored thousands of times (three characters free in 30 rooms: 81 000 position combinations before any flag).

Cutting the game into chapters does not change that, because the first chapter already holds the product; it checks the checkpoints and proves each chapter from every way into it, which is what a long single-character game needs.

The solver's next steps, in order (an outside review, LOG #38): measure where the time goes (engine runs, clones, hashes, queue); a proof-mode frontier without best-first ordering or copied paths; the active character out of the state (each character's actions offered from one canonical state, a switch kept explicit only when it has an effect); **mobility regions** (rooms joined by reversible, silent exits merged into one region per character, moves as macro steps with the route kept for the walkthrough); chapter interfaces projected on what the rest reads; a proof-safe reduction (dependency closure, goal and invariant visibility, deadlocks, a cycle proviso, since the property is "from every reachable state the ending stays reachable"), validated against the explicit search on thousands of generated games with every counter-example replayed on the real engine; then parallel frontiers.

Exit criterion: the 40-room stress game proved with 1, 2 and 3 characters, a state count that no longer grows like the product of positions, no generated game where the reduced and explicit verdicts differ, and a truncation that stays a truncation.

limits.text: In proof mode, states that differ only by the active character are one state, and each state offers every character's actions (`Switch to X › action`) when the switch changes nothing the solver reads; a switch that does stays an explicit step, and invariants are checked on every character's view.
The active character is no longer a factor (positions 18 796 → 112 with three characters), but the stress chains still truncate: each character's exact room and bag now split the states.

rows.heading: After v33-mobility: mobility regions, and the reference proof

limits.text: The proof offers the actions of every room of the region as `Go to <room> › action`; the route is played once per room, every hop checked (it arrives, it changes nothing the solver reads), and one that is not silent restarts the search with exact rooms (`profile.mobility.reason`).

**The open chain is still out of reach, and that is the game, not the abstraction.** Without eras, every character can walk the whole chain and pick up anyone's item: which character carries which item is a real product the proof must cover (20 000-state budget):
Exact reductions cannot remove those states; a game built that way is checked by the witness, the chapter witnesses and the playtests, or by bounding who can carry what.

rows.heading: After v33-chapter-interfaces: one search per chapter, from every boundary state at once

limits.text: A chapter is now proved by **one** search that starts from all its boundary states together and shares what it has seen (a state is safe or not whichever start reached it): it costs the union of what the starts reach, not the sum.

rows.heading: After v33-noop-memo: no partial-order reduction in proofs, a no-op memo instead

limits.text: **The reduction, measured in proof mode.** Sleep sets visit every state but skip edges: an action already tried in a commuting order is not run again.
The proof classifies states by reverse reachability over those edges, so a skipped edge can hide the only way to the goal.

On the era game it does: 20 rooms × 3 characters reports a softlock that the plain proof does not have (40 × 3 too), while skipping under 2% of the engine runs and taking 20–25% longer (`tests/por.test.ts`, "why proof mode keeps the reductions off").
A run that writes nothing the solver hashes is kept with the values it read; the same action on a state with the same values is a no-op too, and is not run.
It relies on the read trace being complete: one skip in 16 is run anyway and compared, and a difference is an error, never a silent skip.

This is an equivalence checked on that corpus, not a proof for every game: a future condition or command that forgets to declare a read would break it, and only a check that runs every skip would catch it (`npm run solve -- --audit-abstractions`, 3.3.1).

rows.heading: 3.3.0, measured on the release (5 October 2026, cache off)

limits.text: The open matrix (characters not confined to an era, items moving freely) still truncates with 2 and 3 characters: see "After `v33-mobility`".

It fails (exit 1) on any difference in the verdict, the broken invariants, whether softlocks exist, or the flags, rooms and places reached; it says `partial` (exit 2) when the explicit search does not fit the budget, because then the verdicts were not compared.

`tests/audit.test.ts` runs the same audit on 120 random games (`tests/gen/random-game.ts`: 2–4 rooms, 1–2 characters, negative `has`, consumption, transfers, counters, `once` / `nth` / `cycle`, nested `if`), and on one game per command and per condition of the DSL (the two tables are checked against the `Cmd` and `Cond` types: a new variant without a sample does not compile).
**A dead flag that was not dead.** The first written rule that matches answers.
A flag that gates only an earlier rule, which itself only touches that flag, looked dead to the liveness analysis, yet it decides whether the earlier rule or a later one answers.
The solver merged the two states and lost every path through the later rule; on one random game, the abstractions happened to reach a flag the explicit search did not.
This was a flaw of the base search, not of an abstraction.
**Rooms reached.** With the canonical character, a room where only another playable character stood was missing from `roomsReached` (and so could be reported by the lint as never reached).

`games/reference`, "The Night Market": 8 rooms, 9 items, 5 characters, two of them playable (Pixel and Biscuit, who hand items to each other and open places for each other), a staged market (Canvas, 960 wide, 6 layers with parallax, 3 occluders, 2 walk zones joined by stairs), a yard on two planes (a ladder opened by a flag, a jump for Biscuit only), an autonomous script, a minigame, a timeline finale.

rows.heading: 3.4.0, measured on the release (5 October 2026, cache off)

limits.text: 3.4 changed the picture, not the logic: every state count is the one 3.3.0 measured; the times move within the noise of a laptop.
So the result depends on the batch and never on the number of workers; one worker is the same batched search in the search's thread.

A worker that cannot start, or stops, leaves its nodes to the search's thread (the result does not change; `profile.workers.reason` says it); the custom commands reach the workers from the game's module; the partial-order reduction keeps them off.
`--time` stops a search, workers or not.

What does not scale: the merge (the states cross between threads, the search's thread checks each one), and starting the workers (about 0.3 s): a small proof, like each of the sample game's chapters, is not faster.
With several playable characters, which one holds an item multiplies the states: three characters and twelve items that move freely is the open matrix that 3.3 could not prove.

An item no condition reads (so lacking it decides nothing: no `else`, no rule shadowed by one that needs it), in no invariant or goal, lost or moved only by an action on it, and given by no rule or reaction by kind (`poolableItems`), is pooled while every two characters can meet: the state keeps how many of each pooled item exist, not who holds them.
One that does not restarts the proof without pooling (`profile.ownership.reason`), like mobility.
The 3.5 target, the 20 × 3 open matrix within budget, is **not met**.
The owner applies only while every two characters can meet, and in the open chain locked doors keep them apart most of the time (1 817 hand-overs in 200 000 states).
As decided, this does not block 3.5; it is the open question for what follows.
**Witness dominance** (`--dominance`, witnesses only: it cannot prune a proof).
A state with no more progress than one already seen (the same everything else; its monotonic items and boolean flags, those nothing reads for their absence, a subset) is not explored.
A witness search that finds nothing with it runs again without it, so it never reports `unsolved` by itself.

The best-first search reaches a witness before a dominated state comes up, and a dominated state only comes up once the better ones are exhausted, which (when absence is never read) means the search is failing anyway.

rows.heading: When the DSL is not enough

limits.text: `effects` says what the command does to the game, as plain commands: they run first, in the browser **and** in the solver, so a custom command never breaks `npm run solve` nor the save.
`run` is the visual part, browser only (it gets the scene element, the presenter, the state to read, the arguments).

`run` must not touch the state: in dev mode the engine compares the state before and after it and reports in the journal a `run` that changed something outside `effects` (the solver, the saves and the replay only know `effects`).
Translating is a table, not keys in the content:
If a room declares an actor for a playable character, that actor stands for them while they are inactive (poses, talk topics); they are not drawn twice.

**Four words, never merged**: `not-run`, `blocked`, `failed`, `passed`.
Only `passed` is done in the release notes, and only `passed` may lift a surface's `experimental` (D18).
A pass is still reported, not blocking, for a 4.1.x tag (D12); `field:check --require=<id,…>` is there for the 4.2 gate.
**What a pass tried says**: an operator (a pseudonym or a role, never an identity), when it started and finished, on what (OS, browser, device or versions) and the scenario.
**Nothing private, as far as a scan can tell**: the schema refuses a field it does not name; a report holding a key, a token, an email address or a bearer is refused.
The leak scan is a hygiene barrier made of patterns, not a proof: it cannot see a secret it has no pattern for, and in an image or a binary it looks for keys and tokens only.

A bundle carries only the evidence its report lists: logs are redacted (addresses, bearers, password values, IPs), a key or a token refuses the bundle, and its `bundle-manifest.json` gives every file's SHA-256.
An open issue is a pass not made.

**Integrity, not authenticity**: a report is checked against the `candidate-manifest.json` beside it, as given; `field:init` downloads it from the run itself (`gh run download`), and a folder whose manifest was edited checks against that edit.
The release's own gate reads the run's manifest, never the folder's.

**Evidence is a file under `evidence/`** (at most 16 MiB, 64 MiB for one report; `field:check` says so before a bundle is tried), read where it is: not a link, not outside the folder once resolved, not an archive (what is inside cannot be read for a leak), never a report or the manifest.
**Another commit, another pass**: a report of another candidate run, or whose file digests are not the candidate's, does not check.

rows.heading: Roadmap: from v1.3 to the 4.1.x line, and 4.2

limits.text: An external audit of web-scumm concluded that the engine can produce a good short point-and-click, but not comfortably a game of 30 to 100 rooms, because it was purely reactive (tap → rule → commands) with no world simulation.

We checked its 18 claims against the code: 12 exact, 4 partial, 2 wrong (`give` / `take` / `room` are not commands; the minigames are not in the core, they are already a registry a game extends from `games/<id>/index.ts`).
This roadmap orders the work by what actually blocks a long game, not by fidelity to Day of the Tentacle.
no autonomous script, no timer, no event: `onEnter` was the only trigger besides a tap; the only loop was the render rAF;

rows.heading: Our take on the audit (kept, changed)

limits.text: **Kept**: scheduler + events + world actors as the first milestone; no rewrite, no Phaser; chapter solver with goals and invariants; multi-slot saves with data-only migrations; a "why is this rule unavailable" debugger; animations with frame events; an escape hatch with effects declared to the solver.
*Events and the scheduler are one feature.* An event bus without scripts able to wait (`waitEvent`, `waitUntil`) is only a renamed flag.
*Several playable characters is not P0* for "anyone makes a complete game": it is P0 only for DOTT.
What is missing is the **visualisation** in the Studio (a tree derived from the topics) and filling known gaps (the Studio cannot add or remove a topic).
Insult sword fighting is an *activity* (minigame), not a dialogue primitive.
Only docs and an example outside the core are missing; not a priority.

*The real risk* is not technical: every added primitive must be understood by `validate`, `solve`, CONTENT_GUIDE en/fr, the prompts generator, the MCP tools and the Studio, otherwise the AI will not use it, or badly.

**Everything stays data**: new commands in the `Cmd` union, new typed fields on `RoomDef` / `GameDef`, never functions in the content (except the `custom` registry, which lives in `index.ts` like the minigames).

limits.text: **World actors**: `GameState.where` (character → room), `CharacterDef.room` (starting room), `{ moveActor: [char, room], at? }`, condition `{ actorIn: [char, room] }`; a moving character only shows in the room it is in; checkpoints take `where`.
An event is not a state: it fires, then is gone; a listener sets a flag when something must be remembered.
Scripts advance one command at a time between the player's actions, never during one, a cutscene, a conversation or a minigame.

**Solver**: "Script <id>" is an action (run until it waits, ends or loops); numeric flags are clamped to the highest threshold a condition compares them with, so a counter script does not create states forever.
**Validator**: unique script ids, loops that never wait, events emitted but never listened to (and the reverse), moving characters without a starting room or without an actor in the target room.
Also: navmesh paths are pulled straight when the shortcut stays inside the walk zone (the hero no longer takes a detour around a corner it does not need).

limits.text: A second audit, on v2.0.1, concluded that the primitives were there and that the next step was proof and tooling, not more commands.
Two of its claims were wrong (`engine.ts` and `types.ts` are under a thousand lines each, not three thousand), its direction was right.

Writing them found three real solver gaps, fixed: it only ever took the last option of a `choice`, it clamped counters that go down (haggling), and it ran a script whole instead of one `wait` at a time (a patrol was never seen in the middle room).
The validator uses it to spot a flag only set by actions that already need it.
**The solver prunes what cannot matter**: from the same graph, a flag nobody but its setter reads, a script whose effects reach nothing live, a walker nobody waits for are left out of the state.

limits.text: The proof: `v33-proof-profile` (where the time goes, `npm run bench -- --matrix`), `v33-proof-core` (a heap frontier and parent pointers: the queue went from 89% of the time to nothing, same witnesses), `v33-player-canonical` (states that differ only by who is active are one state), `v33-mobility` (mobility regions: silent moves folded into the next action, an exact fallback when a move is not silent), `v33-chapter-interfaces` (one shared search per chapter from every boundary state, a goal checked on every character's view: a real bug found against the explicit search), `v33-noop-memo` (the partial-order reduction measured in proof mode and refused: it reported a softlock that does not exist; instead the engine's writes are traced and a try that wrote nothing is not run again on the same read values, every skip checkable), `v33-one-status` (one status, exit code and sentence for the CLI, its JSON, the Studio and the MCP tool), `v33-proof-cache` (a result keyed by the engine, the game and the options, given back when nothing changed).

rows.heading: Verification (every milestone)
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: MCP: `npm run -s mcp` lists the updated tools; a fresh AI session adds a script / event to the demo following only CONTENT_GUIDE.
A search that runs out of a budget (states, time or memory) says `truncated`: nothing is proved then, and the exit code is not 0.
A proof never reads `proved` where a budget cut it.
The engine state is kept only while the node waits to be expanded.
On the open instances of the proof matrix the heap falls 16 to 20 times (1.6 KB a state on o21 instead of 31.6, BENCH.md "4.1.13"); the time per state is the engine's, and does not change.

A proof folds states that differ only in what cannot matter, each fold audited against the explicit search (`npm run solve -- --audit-abstractions`, `npm run audit:corpus` every night): the canonical character (who holds the controls), the mobility regions (rooms one walks between silently), the canonical owner (who holds an item no condition reads), the no-op memo (a try known to change nothing).

Dominance (a state with no more progress than one seen) prunes witnesses only: in a proof it changes verdicts on generated games (`tests/dominance.test.ts`), so it stays off there and the profile says why.
Three counts say what never became a state: symmetries folded, tries that changed nothing, and transitions that landed on a state already seen (two orders of independent actions).
The independent sub-puzzles (groups of dimensions no rule links) are reported, not applied: proving each alone needs a product argument the search does not make.
`--resume` takes it up from that file, to the same verdict and the same witness as a search that never stopped (`tests/checkpoint.test.ts` kills a real process with SIGKILL at 30 % and resumes it).

`--workers=N` expands the frontier a batch at a time on worker threads; the merge stays in the batch's order, so the result depends on the batch, never on the number of workers (`tests/workers.test.ts`, `tests/partition.test.ts`).
The exact keys stay the authority: a worker's "already stored" the search does not confirm is expanded again in the search's thread.
Workers speed an exploration up; they do not answer an explosion of states.
It runs every night, never on a pull request.
Where an instance does not finish, the matrix's gap report says which budget stopped it and which dimension grew.

rows.heading: Speedrun (4.1.14 "Time Attack")
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: A player starts an attempt from the pause menu, the engine times it, splits it on what happens in the game (never on pixels), and seals the run into a `.wsrun` file that anyone can replay and verify.
Nothing here promises to detect every cheat: a replay proves a run is possible and its in-game time exact; only a server's or a human's observation raises the trust further.
Neither stops the in-game time (the game does not run while it waits).

`GameDef.speedrun` (types in `docs/en/API.md`, checked by `npm run validate`), content only: a new category needs no change in the engine (`tests/speedrun-manifest.test.ts` proves it with a fixture game).

`reload` says what a load does: `invalidates` the run, or is `allowed` (a state the run itself reached); `segment` (a load starting a timed segment) is reserved, not implemented in 4.1.14: the validator refuses it.
`seed: 'fixed'` makes every run draw from `fixed:<id>`; `seed` is the run's generator only.
4.1.15's `seed: 'daily' | 'mystery'` without `world` is read as that world (a random run in it) with a warning.
The rules carry their version: a change never requalifies an old run (`rulesVersion` differs: `unsupported-version`).

The validator refuses unknown events, ids that name nothing, a start equal to the finish, a category without an input, a Reality policy without `reality`, a split that is its own ancestor; it warns about a flag never set and a category that does not require `logic`.
Never reproducible, never an authority: a run timed on `rta` replays as valid but stays unranked without a witness.
Think time is not in it.
The run clock (`Engine.runClock`) observes the engine and never writes the state (D24).

rows.heading: Splits, routes, records and the ghost

limits.text: Splits are automatic: each fires once, the first time its trigger matches after the start; a split that never fires is marked missed and the run goes on.
The solver's witness becomes a **logical route** (`kind: 'logical'`): a reference for routing, never a record.

rows.heading: The proof: .wsrun
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: Schema 2 since 4.1.16 (`SpeedrunEnvelopeV2`, ADR 0019): the game, its fingerprint (the game as written, before any world), the engine's, generator's and durations' versions, the category and its rules' version, the run's generator seed (`runSeed`), the exact world played (`variant`, assignments included, never regenerated from a seed) and, for a Daily or Mystery world, the Bridge's signed tokens (`worldEvidence`), the timing (RTA, steps, IGT, active IGT, the declared pauses, menus, background and loads), the splits, the entries in chunks of 500 chained by SHA-256 from `H0` (the rules) to `Hn`, the loads, the inputs used, the Reality signals, the final state's hash and the final proof.
A schema 1 file (4.1.14, 4.1.15) is still read, as a Story run; offered to a Remix category it is refused (`legacy-world-missing`), never requalified from its seed.

The verifier reloads the category from the game, checks the run's world against the game (`loadVariant`) and its category (`worldVerdict`, the day's token or the Mystery commitment and reveal checked with the key `remix.daily` names), rebuilds that world, replays the entries with the run's seed (the random draws are drawn again, never taken from the file), recomputes the clock, the splits, the final state and the chain, then checks the rules, and names the leaderboard the run goes to (`world.leaderboardKey`: the category, and for Fixed and Daily the seed).
`inconclusive` is never valid.

`local` (timed by the player's machine) → `replay-valid` (a verifier other than the client replayed it) → `server-witnessed` (the server dated the run's chunks as they were played: reserved, not in 4.1.14) → `moderator-verified` (a human with the leaderboard's admin token looked at it).
Only someone other than the client raises a level; an envelope that claims more is read as `local`.

It does not prove that a person produced those answers, that `inputsUsed`, the pauses or the RTA are complete, that a printed wheel was used, or that the envelope was not made outside the player: that is `server-witnessed` or `moderator-verified`, never "anti-cheat".

The reference chapter's `wheel-proved` category wants the wheel won and proved whenever it is played (the wheel stays optional: a route that never opens the map does not play it); its other categories keep 4.1.16's rule.

rows.heading: Reality policies
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: `live`: the same proof, in a category of its own (the latency and the availability of a live signal are not reproducible).
Without the keys the verifier cannot conclude (`no-keyring`).
Local tools on the player's machine (D23), never on the Bridge, never in the PWA.
The tools accept events from the game's origin only (the dev server and the preview by default, `--origin=<url>` for a deployed build): another page open in the browser cannot post fake splits.

rows.heading: Leaderboards on the Bridge
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: Every instance's workers share one queue: a run is **created once** (its key is unique: two instances receiving the same run create one), **claimed by one worker** under a lease, and **claimed again** when its worker died and the lease expired; a worker that lost its lease cannot store a verdict.

Each worker is an **isolated process** (`tools/speedrun/worker.ts`): a bounded heap, killed with its process group at its time budget, an environment holding only `PATH`, the game package's folder and the heap size (no secret of the Bridge), fetch, WebSocket, TCP, UDP and DNS refused in-process (defence in depth, not a sandbox: see REALITY-OPS, "The speedrun worker"), the package checked against its approved fingerprint, its answer signed with a one-time key.
The HTTP process never replays.
A run is identified by its game, category, run seed and inputs (their RTA stamps aside), never by its world: the first submitter keeps it, a copy re-stamped or re-sealed in another world is refused.

A client may submit ten runs a minute (`perMinute`), every instance together under `bridge serve` on a SQL store (one bucket per client in the database, keyed by an HMAC of the address, never the address; a library host without a SQL limiter counts per instance); a duplicate or an invalid run costs a token, a refusal says `Retry-After`.

The queue holds at most `maxQueued` runs waiting or being verified, counted and written in one step for every instance (4.1.17: two instances seeing 99 of 100 no longer both write); the envelope is dropped once the verdict is stored; old runs are purged hourly.

`GET /v1/runs?game=&category=[&key=][&limit=]` is a leaderboard: valid runs only, each **pseudonym's** best (the Bridge knows no player identity: two people who choose the same pseudonym are one line), on the **verifier's key** (`world.leaderboardKey`: the category, and for a Fixed or Daily world `<category>:<seed>`); equal times share a rank, then the earlier submission comes first.
A Daily run sent after its day is practice (valid, not ranked); a Mystery run is `valid-unranked` without a server witness.

Since 4.1.17 the Remix menu has a **Mystery world** entry: it asks the game's Bridge for a commitment, then its reveal, verifies both offline with the game's daily key, builds the world and keeps both tokens beside it; a speedrun started in it (within the minute the reveal allows: after it the page says so and does not start the run) carries them and its start time.

The worker is meant to replay an older run with that release's archive (pinned version); in 4.1.14 the verifier replays its own version only and says `unsupported-version` (`engine-version`) for another one.
**Anonymity**: a leaderboard shows a pseudonym (2 to 32 letters, digits, spaces, `_ . -`; an email is refused) and never anything else about the player.
Pseudonyms are **not authenticated**: anyone may submit under any name, and anyone may submit a published run first under theirs.
**Ghosts on semantic targets**: a ghost shows rooms, actions on ids and the inventory, never a pixel trail; it is off the first time a category is played.

rows.heading: Accessibility and fairness
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: An accessibility option is **never an implicit cheat**: the text speed, the text size, reduced motion and the readable font change nothing in the in-game time (a line costs the same logical time at every speed), and the keyboard's and the screen reader's targets are the same actions.
**Integrity is not authenticity**: the chain proves a file was not altered after it was sealed, not that the client was honest; a client can recompute it.

**`replay-valid` admits tool-assisted runs**: a run whose inputs a script or the solver chose replays valid (the committed reference run is the solver's route), and so does a run resumed after a crash (the inputs lost after its last chunk are not in its time).
Only a witness or a moderator rules them out.

Not in 4.1.14: the live witness (`server-witnessed`), the pinned-version replay in the worker, a SQL store for the runs, the `/v1/runs` mount in `bridge/src/server.ts`, the cross-browser e2e (`npm run e2e:speedrun`) in CI, real OBS and LiveSplit sessions and field tests by speedrunners (human passes).

rows.heading: Studio Server: one game, several people, online

limits.text: The app's disk is a cache: Clever Cloud's disk does not survive a restart, and nothing is lost when it goes.
**The game's code never runs in the Studio**: validating it and reading it go to `studio-worker`, a second app that holds no password, key or database access (ADR 0028).
**The game is played on another origin** (`playUrl`): its code cannot act with a member's Studio session.

rows.heading: Deploying on Clever Cloud
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: Only the studio app is linked to the add-ons: **never link them to the worker.** Both apps build from the repository's root: leave `APP_FOLDER` unset (an app that held another project may still have one: `clever env rm APP_FOLDER`).
Two `*.cleverapps.io` names are two sites: the game's cookie then lives in a frame of another site only because it is partitioned (CHIPS).
The Studio shows them to members and every preview plays them; they are read only on a hosted Studio.

rows.heading: From the release archives
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: Their versions are locked in its `npm-shrinkwrap.json` and its SBOM; npm reads that lock when it installs from the registry, not from an archive file, where `pg` takes the latest 8.x its range allows (`quest-n-click-studio-server deps` says which).

rows.heading: The OpenID provider
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: It must differ from the `studio` client's id: an id_token is never accepted as an access token.
`users`: your own, or none (Keycloak's console adds them), each with a verified email and a password that is not the file's.
The admin API does not take that password through the master realm's `admin-cli` (`401 invalid_client`): `kcadm.sh` and scripts built on it fail as they are.

rows.heading: People and roles
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: The Play tab's **Publish this revision** has the worker build the player's game from the head (no editing tools), numbered: build `#n` is served at `/play/<n>/` on the game's origin and never changes.

An owner's **Rebuild fresh** builds the same snapshot again, against the same assets' version, and says whether the files are the same, byte for byte: a check that the build is reproducible on the worker as it is now, not that its content is harmless.
A build's code never changes; its images and sounds are the instance's prepared assets, served beside it as they are now.
A published build has no service worker (it is not installed for offline play) and its saves are not yet told apart by build.
Reviewers comment too: comments are kept by the Studio (in its database, in the backup), never in a game file, so no game file is written for them.

A comment whose anchor the game no longer names (its rooms, rules, scripts, entities, objectives and checkpoints, the storyboard's boards and panels) is said "orphan", never attached elsewhere; a line's id is not an anchor.
A public https or a local remote needs none; a remote URL never carries credentials.

**Push** (an owner): one commit of the revisions confirmed since the last push, the game's files at the head in `path`, each author of those revisions a `Co-authored-by` (their email, or their name at a mailbox that does not exist); the rest of the repository is left as it is.
**Never forced.** A branch that moved since the Studio's last push (someone pushed there) is refused (409), and so is a branch that exists but the Studio never imported: import it first.
It replaces what the Studio had not pushed (still in its history).
A link, a submodule, or a file the game cannot hold refuses the whole import.

The Studio never checks a working tree out: a push builds its commit from objects, an import reads the commit's objects, so the repository's links, attributes and ignore rules cannot reach the server's files.
The game's `private/` never goes to the repository, and an import leaves it as it is.
An author's email goes in a `Co-authored-by` only when the provider verified it; otherwise their name at `users.noreply.<the Studio's host>`.

rows.heading: Upgrading the engine of a hosted game

limits.text: A game imported from a 4.1.x project that never ran `quest-n-click migrate` is still at authoring schema 2 (no `schemaVersion: 3`, no stable ids).

Nothing is written yet, and nothing but those files: the Studio refuses an answer that names another file, or a file the game does not have (the game's code runs before the migration and could shape it).

A game the migration would break (an id the tool could not write, a list built by code, a game that can no longer be finished), or that the solver cannot judge in time, is refused with a 422 (`errors`, `skipped`: what the tool could not write) and the head stays as it was: migrate it on a local Studio (`quest-n-click migrate`, then `npm run ids` to see what is left) and import it again, or fix it first.

**The former name (4.3.0, D47).** A game that still imports `web-scumm/…` does not load on a 4.3.0 Studio (the aliases are gone): its health is not green and the guard refuses its writes (a 422: the game still does not load).
The solver does not judge it, so a game that cannot be finished yet is never stuck.
The rename is written without an undo (it would bring back imports that no longer resolve), so the owner's earlier history stays reachable; a backup taken before is the way back.
A worker that refuses, times out or leaves no result while the guard asks never counts as the game not loading: the write fails (503) and the next one asks again.
The project's `tsconfig.json` (`baseUrl`, which `quest-n-click migrate` also fixes) is not part of a hosted game and is left alone.

rows.heading: Backup and restore
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: `/readyz` gives `rpoMs`, the age of the oldest operation not shipped yet (0 when everything is): the target is 1 min (D42), measured, never claimed.
The line is `0`, then new after each restore: the revisions a restored instance writes again never overwrite the segments of the timeline it left.

**A backup**: `npm run studio-server -- backup <file> --config <file>` writes the project's tables in one snapshot (members, the journal, the head, the previews, builds and prepared sets; not the sessions nor the leases: a restore logs everyone out; only confirmed operations), with the blobs they name and a digest.
Its digest says it is whole, not who made it; keep it where only operators write.

**To the bucket** (4.2.3): `npm run studio-server -- backup --to-bucket --keep 14 --config <file>` writes it to the instance's bucket as `backups/<date>-r<revision>.json` (UTC, `2026-10-19T03-17-00Z`), then deletes the backups it wrote past the 14 most recent (never another object).
It survives the database, not the bucket: a copy elsewhere is yours to make.

**A restore**: a hosted instance only, into an empty database (a new Postgres add-on, the same bucket): `npm run studio-server -- restore <file> --replay --config <file>` checks the digest, the tables and columns, and that every blob of the head and of the journal is in the bucket (a preview, build or prepared set whose blobs were collected since is left out, and counted as `dropped`), writes the rows, then replays the journal shipped since the backup.

Each replayed operation must continue the head (its revision, each file's previous content, its blobs); the replay stops at the first that does not (`stopped`: `gap`, `not-the-head`, `blob-missing`…).

The head's and the journal's blobs are never collected (the journal keeps every operation); an older backup restored after a collection only loses the previews, builds and prepared sets the collection took.

rows.heading: Running it: the reference deployment
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: **Deploy, and upgrade the engine: an overlapping redeploy.** `clever deploy` (or a push) starts the new instance while the old one still serves: measured by spike S (`docs/dev/SPIKE-4.2.1-CLEVER.md` §2), where the old instance also never logged its SIGTERM.
Since 4.2.3 the new instance does not wait for that: once it listens it asks for the lease, and the holder gives it back at its next renewal (10 s at most), logging `lease-lost`.

**between two versions that both hand the lease over** (two redeploys of the same commit): `lease-taken` 6 and 10 s after the new instance listened; then writes are 503 (`Retry-After: 2`) for 10 to 16 s, because Clever still sends the requests to the old instance, which no longer holds the lease, until the deploy ends; before that, while the new instance starts, a write may wait 10 to 20 s on its journal check and get a 503 too.
It is never behind the session and never on the game's origin, where any request without the game's session is refused before its path is read (a 401, "open the game from the Studio").
| `studio_worker_jobs_in_flight` | the jobs asked of the worker and not answered yet: the queue as the Studio sees it |
| `studio_journal_rpo_seconds` | the age of the oldest operation not shipped to the bucket (the `rpoMs` of `/readyz`) |
The worker's own queue is not measured from the worker: the Studio's side of it is.
OpenTelemetry is not supported in 4.2.3; it stays an option for later.
It does not read `/metrics`: a scraper you run does (Prometheus with its Alertmanager, or any service that reads the format), or a simple prober for `/readyz`.
`/readyz` is not 200 for 2 min (no instance serves writes; a deploy keeps it at 503 for about 20 s, above; the first deploy onto 4.2.3 for about 2.5 min: expect that alert then);
`studio_lease_conflicts_total` jumps (people waiting on each other's spans: not a fault, a sign to look at);

**The daily backup.** The repository carries `clevercloud/cron.json`: at 03:17 UTC every day it runs `ops/studio/backup-cron.sh`, which does nothing unless the app sets `STUDIO_BACKUP_CRON=1`, and nothing on another instance than number 0 (Clever runs a repository's crons on every app and every instance deployed from it: set the variable on the studio app only, never the worker).

From the release archives (which do not carry the script), copy `ops/studio/backup-cron.sh` into your app with its last line as `exec npx quest-n-click-studio-server backup --to-bucket --keep "${STUDIO_BACKUP_KEEP:-14}"`, make it executable, and point your `clevercloud/cron.json` at it: `["17 3 * * * $ROOT/backup-cron.sh"]`.
Clever runs a cron with no environment unless its script starts with `#!/bin/bash -l`, and with absolute paths only (`$ROOT` is the app's folder).
Never the production one: a restore refuses a database that holds anything, but check anyway.

Check, read-only, on both databases (`psql <URI>`): `SELECT value FROM studio_meta WHERE key = 'revision'` gives the head noted in step 1 (or later, if people wrote meanwhile), and `SELECT path, blob FROM studio_files ORDER BY path` gives the same rows at the same revision.
Never run `gc --delete` from the drill's database: it would collect the blobs production still names.

rows.heading: Working together
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: If someone else wrote one of its files since, the write is refused (409) with that file as you read it and as it is now (the writes since of the same tab, CLI or MCP session never refuse it; your other tab's, or an agent's of yours, do).

Limits: the check is per file (two notes edited at once are one file); the room view's placement is checked against what the Rooms tab read, while the view may still show an older preview for a moment; a script that sends no `x-studio-base` is not checked this way.
**Undo is yours** (4.2.2): Undo and Redo (and Ctrl/Cmd+Z, Shift for redo) undo your own last operation, whatever the others wrote meanwhile, as a new revision (history is never rewritten).
The tokens are kept in `~/.config/web-scumm/studio-tokens.json` (0600), and only sent over https.

It is a starting point, not a turnkey setup: with OIDC you still need a configuration with `oidc.allowInsecure: true` (a provider over http), a MinIO bucket, a worker (`npm run studio-worker`) and `trustProxy`.
Docker is never required.
The server also runs without OIDC, with SQLite and a folder for the contents, on the loopback only.

The game in the Studio is the preview of a revision (4.2.2): after each change the worker builds the head (a burst of changes builds its last revision only), and the room view loads it once built, unless a placement is not saved.
Meanwhile the frames show the last ready preview, and the label under the room view says which revision it is, the one building, and a revision that does not build, with its reason.
A preview is built from the game's text files only (sources, data): a game whose code imports a stylesheet or an image cannot be previewed.

A read's revision is the journal's head: an instance that does not hold the lease yet (a deploy) may answer from a folder behind it, and a new history (an import, a restore) is not told apart from an older revision.

When a revision fails where the last judged one passed, a bisection over the revisions between them names the first that fails, with what its operation did and its files (never who made it), in at most ⌈log₂ n⌉ judgements; a dev can ask for one between two revisions at or before the head (`POST /api/health/bisect {good, bad}`).
A solver cut short says "unknown", never "valid", and stops a bisection; a revision that fails to be judged five times says "cannot be judged", with its reason.
An older verdict is shown greyed, never green.

Each revision asks it for three jobs: a preview's build, the validator and a solver run (up to 45 s); the preview no longer waits behind the other two, and the next change's validation can still wait for them.

A preview, since 4.4.0: one snapshot per revision is packed (under the lock, the folder repaired) and shared by the preview, the health, the published builds and the engine's upgrade, given again while the head has not moved; its files are stored 8 at a time, and a blob this instance stored less than an hour ago is not written again (its date is already well within the collection's day of grace, and its key is its content's hash); the Studio answers as soon as it has read the worker's result, its staging deleted after.
Vite's cache is not kept between jobs: a `vite build` does not use it (it holds the dev server's prebundled dependencies), and a folder the game's code writes in must not outlive its job (ADR 0028).

An upload (a sound, a decor) is 10 MiB at most once decoded (413 past it) and its type is read from its bytes: a PNG, JPEG or WebP image (a decor: PNG or JPEG), an Ogg, MP3 or WAV sound whose extension says the same (415 otherwise; a local Studio also takes M4A, FLAC, AAC, Opus and WebM); it is written as one operation, never run.

A sheet's cutting and a cell's keying run on the worker (`cut` jobs, Python with the hook's packages, no game code), under the project's exclusive lease: the worker gets the image, that sheet's cells and `site.json`, gives back only cells of that sheet, and the cells with the backups of those recut are written as one operation.
A hosted Studio does not keep the uploaded sheet itself (a local one keeps it under `private/sheets/`, which no span names).
Published builds serve the prepared set as it is now, not the one they were built against.

`POST /api/jobs/<id>/cancel` (who started it, or an owner) cancels it: a waiting job never runs; a running one has its request to the worker closed, and the worker kills its child with its process group; nothing is written (no operation, no prepared set kept) and the exclusive lease is given back.
Captures are not available on a hosted Studio.
The Play tab shows the game with its DEV panel; the state inspector, the rule explainer and the replays beside it need the game on the Studio's origin, so the local Studio only.
The Assistant is not on a hosted Studio yet.
The Studio's editors do not yet send the revision of what they read (the journal checks it when sent): within a span you hold, your save replaces the file.
Editors reload what others commit, so this matters only for an edit begun just before a span changed hands.
The room editor's own Save does nothing on a hosted Studio: "Save layout" in the Studio saves (the editor's page is the game's, and only the member starts a write).
A game that imports files outside its own folder cannot run on the worker.

rows.heading: Studio: local WYSIWYG authoring, and the open door for any AI

limits.text: `npm run studio` and `npm run dev` listen on `127.0.0.1`: another machine cannot reach their file-writing routes.
Do not expose the development port to the Internet.
A provider call never follows a redirect, gives up after 60 s, and reads at most 8 MB of answer.
Game TypeScript and custom commands are trusted code, not sandboxed data.

rows.heading: Layout of the Studio
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: Selecting one (in the list or in the view) opens its sheet: name, kind, states, visibility, **look lines** (add, edit, delete), **reactions** (verb, targets, condition, commands as a list of lines: texts editable, other commands shown), **talk topics** (as a list, or as a **tree**: topics, lines, choices and their options, branches, each with its condition; tapping a node jumps to its editor); next to every cutscene, arrival script and world script, a **Timeline** toggle draws how long each command takes and what overlaps (lines, walks, animations, parallel branches, the player's turns in red; tap a bar to jump to its line); under the view, the room's name, **hints**, **on enter** lines, the room's **scripts** and **events** (read-only structure, texts editable).

**Storyboard** (see below): the saved storyboard is checked against the content after every load and save (`src/engine/tools/coverage.ts`): a badge on each board and panel (✓ everything is in the game, ~ partly, ✗ something is missing, ? prose), and under a panel the list of what is not there yet (an action no rule answers, a line the game does not say, a sound not in `audio.sfx`); the bar shows the overall score.

Each revision is the game folder with the journal's later operations undone, built as a preview (the worker's child, never the Studio's process) and drawn in headless Chromium at 960 × 600 (one device pixel, reduced motion, no CSS animation, fonts loaded, the editor's overlays hidden).

Limits: a local Studio only (`npm run studio`; a hosted Studio answers 501, its worker has no browser); the game's default language; the room as it is entered (its first checkpoint, else a fresh state), not at a checkpoint you choose; the prepared images, sounds and fonts of today on both sides (a changed picture is not shown until it is prepared, then on both sides); a hand edit the journal did not record is in both sides; a channel off by 16 or less is the same pixel (an anti-aliased edge moves by 2 between two renders).

Two toggles above the graph: **Critical path** fades everything that does not lead to the end, a goal or an invariant; **Heat** colours each rule, topic, listener, script and room by how many times the solver went through it.

Above it, **Playtests** (dev server only): the sessions of `games/<id>/playtests/` replayed and summed up, and the puzzle graph's "Heat" selector can colour the nodes by the players' sessions instead of the solver's runs.
The engine keeps it only in dev mode (`Engine.trace`, the last 200 entries).

For a game with `speedrun` (4.1.14, `docs/en/SPEEDRUN.md`), the **speedrun** panel: the categories and their rules, the splits with an editor (name, trigger; **+ split**; **Write to the game** writes the manifest with `set_value` on `@game`), **Preview on this session** (the frame's session replayed with the category's splits: the times a run would record), **Export route** / **Import route** (`.wsroute`), **Logical route (solver)** (the witness, never a record), the last two routes compared, and **Export run (.wsrun)** once an attempt in the frame is sealed.
The Rooms tab keeps the raw braces in its text editor and, under a text holding a switch, a read-only line: the text as a player reads it with the values picked here (`(form=?)` while none is).
The local Studio only: a hosted Studio's game runs on its own origin (set the flag in the game's DEV panel).
A manifest that cannot make a world shows the validator's reasons.
Computed with the engine's compiler (`src/studio/remix-model.ts`): the Studio never shows a world the player would not play.

**Map** (4.2.3): the scenario's groupings, chapters, puzzles and characters (`games/<id>/groupings.json`), each a list of what the game already names (a room, a rule or topic id, `item:<id>`, `char:<id>`, `objective:<id>`, `checkpoint:<id>`) with the `file:line` that writes it, or "not declared" when the game does not know it; then the rooms, characters, items, objectives and checkpoints no grouping names yet (ids written by code, and line or step ids, are not in the IR's provenance: they show as "not declared").
A grouping only refers: saving it writes `groupings.json` alone, never the content.
The map is derived at each read (from the IR's provenance and the groupings), never stored.
The forms come from one table of every condition and command (`src/studio/schema.ts`, checked against the types at compile time): a new command without a form does not compile.

**Layers, masks, zones (4.1.11).** Under the room sheet, the stage editor (`src/studio/rooms-stage.ts`) shows the backdrop with the occlusion masks (red), the walk zones (green) and the links between zones: each layer's depth, parallax, opacity and blend are fields; **Draw a mask** and **Draw a zone** take the corners clicked on the backdrop, then **Close the polygon** (one that closes no surface is not kept); **Link them** joins two zones by a stairs, ladder, jump, teleport or walk link placed by two clicks.

limits.text: `solve` exits 2 when its state budget is exhausted: that is `truncated`, never a proof.

**Lint.** `npm run lint` says what `validate` cannot (it checks shapes and references) and what `solve` does not say loudly (it answers "can it be finished"): from the puzzle graph, a condition nothing sets (`cond-never-true`, an error), a rule another rule matches first (`rule-shadowed`), an item no rule needs (`item-red-herring`) or nothing gives (`item-never-gained`), a hint that waits for something nothing sets (`hint-stuck`, an error) or shares its `until` with an earlier hint (`hint-never-fires`), a dead topic, choice option or listener, a choice with one option, an exit with a condition and no `locked` line, an action that only changes what nothing live reads (`action-dead`, info; a flag a character's variant or a text switch reads is not counted as nothing, so the intro's choice of the hero is not reported), two or more values of the hero's flag that no hero variant matches, so those heroes look like the written one (`hero-looks-default`, info; CONTENT_GUIDE, "Choosing the hero"), a target standing behind a walk link a condition closes whose rule does not check that condition (`walk-link-gate`: the link stops the walk, never the action); after a solver run, a required signal's fallback the closed witness never plays (`fallback-unplayed`, a warning), a live action the witness never ran and a room it never entered (`rule-never-run`, `room-never-reached`: info with the witness, warnings with a completed `--prove`; a truncated proof keeps them as information and says so, it never calls anything unreachable), and a live action that ran without ever changing the state (`rule-no-effect`, info: a topic that only talks, or a `set` already true).
Reachability counts every try the solver made, whether or not it changed the state.
Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 an error that is not ignored, 2 the search was truncated (`--json` carries `status` and `truncated`).

**Proof cache.** A solver run depends only on the engine's code, the game (content, layouts, custom commands, and the game folder's sources) and the options: `npm run solve` (every mode), `--chapters` and `npm run lint` keep each result in `.cache/proofs/` and give it back when none of that changed, saying so (`(from the proof cache, key …)`; `cached` in `--json`).
`--no-cache` or `PROOF_CACHE=0` runs again; `PROOF_CACHE_DIR` moves it; an engine error is never kept.
Tests call the solver directly and never use it.
| `softlocks` | 1 | reachable states from which it can no longer be reached (`softlockCount`, `softlockCauses`) |
| `unsolved` | 1 | it is not reached from any state explored |
| `checkpoint_mismatch` | 1 | chapters only: every chapter proved, but a checkpoint is none of its reachable boundary states |

An e2e only passes when the solver's run is `solved` (its exit code, status and steps are checked) and the engine itself reports the ending (`state.done`): a truncated or unsolved game is a failure, never "the best path replayed anyway".
**Playtests.** On a phone, the pause menu's **Share session** sends the session as a file (Web Share, else a download): ids and indices only, no text, no journal.
`verify:game` runs it without `--strict`, so the CI replays every committed playtest and a content change never blocks a push.

`npm run validate` checks a game that has the file (every asset covered by exactly one entry: two entries matching the same asset are an error, whatever their order; every entry complete); `npm run validate -- --release` requires the file, and a placeholder is an error unless a `releaseExceptions: [{ match, reason }]` entry names that asset (an exception never covers a placeholder added later).
`validate --release` then fails on a file that changed, an asset shipped since, a missing file or an entry edited since the review; a plain `validate` only warns.
`assetBudgets: { initialKB, roomKB, chapterKB }` in `game.ts` are the limits; over one, or a file missing, exits 1.

`initialJsKB` (3.9): the gzipped JavaScript a first visit runs (the entry and its static imports), measured on the build by `npm run verify:dist`, not by `weight`: the minigames, the dev panel and the Studio load on demand (`src/engine/BOUNDARIES.md`).
`--release` (a step of `verify:release`) also fails when a budget is not set.
What an exception lets through is printed by name as accepted, not as a warning to fix.
**A commercial release.** A green `verify:release` does not mean every asset may be sold: an exception is a reason, not a licence.
It checks that the claims are complete and allow a sale, not that they are true.

So every build ends with `tools/dist.ts seal` (a Vite plugin): the assets that are not this game's are removed, and `dist/licenses/` is written: the engine's `LICENSE`, `LICENSE-ASSETS` (the game's own if it has one), `CREDITS.md` from its provenance, `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt` (the licence of every package the bundle took code from, Workbox's for the service worker, the fonts' OFL) and `assets-manifest.json` (each file: path, author, source, licence, SHA-256, status).
The dossier's format (`ticket`, `headline`, `message`, `photos`, `lines`, `outcome`) never changes: a dossier.bin already sealed stays valid.

**Additive.** A speedrun category may name its world (`world: { policy, mode, fixedSeed?, codeWheel? }`, D29); 4.1.15's `seed: 'daily' | 'mystery'` without `world` is read as that world, with a validator warning.

A minigame's result is recorded (`SessionEntry.mg`) and written in the reserved flag `minigame.<id>` (a command never sets one: the validator refuses it); in the player every minigame played leaves that flag in the save.

**A break for hosts that wrote their own `RunStore`** (Bridge library): `board(tenantId, gameId, categoryId, key, limit)` is `board(query: LeaderboardQuery)` and returns ranked rows `{ run, rank }` (each pseudonym's best, ties sharing a rank, then the limit); `admit(run, maxQueued)` (`created | duplicate | full`, one step under the tenant's lock) is new and is what `RunQueue.submit` calls.

**For maintainers.** The people's passes are Field Kit reports (`npm run field:init|check|report|bundle`, `docs/en/FIELD.md`) and open `field-pass` issues; the release notes count only `passed` as done.

`backup` writes **schema 3** (ADR 0021): one read-only snapshot of every tenant, run and daily record, with the backend, the Bridge and SQL schema versions, the counts and a SHA-256 of the payload, written to a temporary file then renamed.
`ops/qualify/`'s Caddy runs unprivileged and read-only.
The first keeps its name but changes meaning: it describes the **engine package** as a game installs it (Vite and its tools included), no longer the repository root's runtime dependencies.
The locks of the Bridge and the connectors live in `scripts/locks/` (`npm run locks`, then commit); a lock that no longer fits its `package.json` stops `pack`.
The Vite configuration no longer loads the Studio; a plugin of yours that imported Studio code from `vite.config.ts` loads it through the dev server.
Files of schemas 1 to 3 are still read, for `--mode=merge` only: nothing under their digest says that they hold every family, so `replace-store` refuses them.
Two backups of the same store no longer share a digest, since it covers their dates.
**A 4.1.19 Bridge cannot read a schema 4 file**: going back to 4.1.19 after a backup taken by 4.1.20 needs a backup taken by 4.1.19 (or `pg_dump`).
**Stop every Bridge older than 4.1.20 before the first restore**: an older Bridge takes no lease and would not be seen.
From 4.2.0 on, strict SemVer: a 4.2.x only fixes, a 4.x minor only adds.
What 4.2.0 calls stable, limited or experimental is in `docs/en/SUPPORT.md` (D38).
Deploy this worker from the repository: installed from the archives, it cannot run `prepare` in 4.2.2 (4.2.3 ships the lock).
A script that writes may send it to be refused (409) rather than write over a change it never saw; without it, it is not checked this way.
**`POST /api/assets/prepare` answers 202 with a job**, no longer the prepared run: a script polls `GET /api/jobs/<id>` until `done`, `failed` or `cancelled`, and reads the run in `result`.

**The daily backup (optional)**: `clevercloud/cron.json` runs `ops/studio/backup-cron.sh` on every app deployed from the repository; it backs up only where `STUDIO_BACKUP_CRON=1` is set (the studio app, never the worker), keeping `STUDIO_BACKUP_KEEP` backups (14 by default).
The new fields are optional and presentation only (D46: no schema, save envelope or IR change):

**The old names keep working through 4.2.x.** Each release of the line also publishes `web-scumm-<version>.tgz`, `create-web-scumm-<version>.tgz`, `web-scumm-bridge-<version>.tgz`, `web-scumm-connectors-<version>.tgz` and `web-scumm-studio-server-<version>.tgz`: the same files at the same version, only the package's name is the old one.
**The formats keep their names.** They are identifiers inside files and stores, not the project's name: renaming them would break existing saves, files and deployments.

The sample game's and the reference chapter's credits now say quest'n'click: their presentation fingerprint moved, so their reference run is recorded again; a game's own fingerprint moves only if its own text changes.

Nothing to change in a game's content: the content format only grows (ADR 0022, D49), `schemaVersion` stays 3, saves and the save envelope are 4.2.0's, the logic fingerprint of a game that uses none of what follows does not move.
**`npm run lint`** has `hero-looks-default` (info), and no longer calls `action-dead` a rule that only sets a flag a character's variant or a text switch reads.

**A Bridge checks the `limits` of its `config.json` at start** (4.3.0): an unknown name, or a value that is not an integer of at least 0 (at least 1 for `streamPage`, `bodyBytes` and `streamBufferBytes`), stops it with the name and the value; on a shared Bridge that is every tenant.

Before upgrading, list each tenant's limits and compare them with `DEFAULT_LIMITS`'s names (`bridge/src/config.ts`): `node -e 'console.log(JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync(process.argv[1], "utf8")).limits ?? {})' <dir>/config.json`.

There is no `web-scumm-<version>.tgz`, `create-web-scumm`, `web-scumm-bridge`, `web-scumm-connectors` or `web-scumm-studio-server` archive any more, no `web-scumm`, `web-scumm-bridge`, `web-scumm-connector`, `web-scumm-studio-server` or `web-scumm-studio-worker` command, and `web-scumm/content` and the other old imports no longer resolve.
Any string that starts with `web-scumm/` in quotes is renamed, an import or not; `web-scumm-save` and the other format names are not.
A symbolic link out of the project, a `web-scumm` script beside a `quest-n-click` one, or a dependency on an old package whose new one is not installed is said and left to you.

A game on a hosted Studio that still imports `web-scumm/…` no longer loads (its health is not green and its writes are refused) until its owner runs the engine's upgrade (`POST /api/engine/migrate`, STUDIO-SERVER).

The upgrade renames its imports first, as a revision of its own judged only by whether the game loads (and, if it loaded before, by no new validator error), never by the solver: a game that cannot be finished yet gets its imports renamed and loads again; then the schema's migration, if one is due, is judged as before and may still be refused (422, the rename kept).
The rename is not undoable (its undo would bring back imports that no longer resolve): take a backup first to go back.
Their output does not change (the sample game's images come out byte for byte the same); a host that installs the worker from `ops/studio/worker-requirements.lock` gets the new wheel by its sha256.

**Voices of a translation**: when a translation adds a text switch its source line has not (`Prêt{form?witch=e|*=} ?` for `Ready?`), `npm run voices -- import` now takes that language's clips by value, `status` no longer calls them orphans, and `npm run validate` warns when one is missing.
Without it a tap only walks, as before.

Il n'écoute pas : dis-le, et dis à l'humain quoi vérifier à l'oreille.

| FM6 | drums (DAC) | grosse caisse / caisse claire / toms ; une partie FM s'il n'y a pas de batterie |

rows.heading: Des stems pour le directeur musical (3.5)

limits.text: `npm run audio -- stems <projet>/spec.json` rend l'arrangement canal par canal (la sortie par canal de Furnace) et additionne les canaux en stems : les `"stems": { "<nom>": ["FM1", "PSG1"], … }` de la spec, ou par rôle de canal s'il n'y en a pas (melody : lead et echo ; harmony : double, harmony, counter, accent, arp ; bass ; drums : le DAC et le bruit).
Un seul gain, le même pour chaque stem, amène la somme à −14 LUFS (jamais une normalisation par stem : l'équilibre est celui de l'arrangement).

La commande écrit `games/<id>/audio/music/<slug>-stems/<stem>.mp3` et un `score.json` à coller sous `audio.scores`, sous l'id du mix unique (le tempo est mesuré sur le rendu : mesures × temps sur sa durée ; `pcmBytes` est le poids décodé des stems à 48 kHz, sur lequel décide un navigateur qui ne donne pas sa mémoire, 3.5.1).
Regrouper les canaux selon ce que le jeu allumera ou éteindra : le thème du jeu d'exemple a mélodie, cordes, harpe et basse, et ne joue que la harpe et la basse quand Biscuit est actif.

rows.heading: Répliques avec des aiguillages de texte (4.3.0)

limits.text: **Un flag pas encore posé** (la réplique est dite avant le choix) : pas de recherche par clé, l'id seul.

**Le validateur** avertit quand une réplique doublée (un clip sous son id ou sous une de ses clés) avec des aiguillages n'a pas le clip d'une valeur listée ; l'id seul joue en attendant, donc un jeu peut sortir avant que tout soit enregistré.
`{hero}` seul n'est pas un aiguillage : une réplique qui dit le nom du héros dans un jeu à plusieurs héros a un seul clip ; écris `{form?m=Max|f=Fay}` quand il faut l'enregistrer par héros.
**Les fichiers** : les clés ne sont que des clés de table.

Le fichier que chacune nomme s'écrit à la main (`'grandma_saw_f.mp3'`), et `npm run assets` comme le lecteur construisent les chemins depuis le fichier, jamais depuis la clé : `~` et `=` n'arrivent jamais dans un nom de fichier ni dans une URL d'asset.

limits.text: La v2.3 lui fait faire trois fois moins d'exécutions du moteur pour les mêmes états : une action qu'aucune règle écrite ne peut répondre (quelles que soient les conditions) ne peut que retomber sur une ligne Regarder, une réaction par kind ou le repli, donc elle n'est plus exécutée du tout (le profil les compte en *skipped*).

rows.heading: Ce que le solveur fait d'un gros jeu
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: Avant la v2.1 le solveur hachait chaque flag, chaque objet et chaque position de script : la version à dix lieux de ce jeu, avec ses horloges, ses promeneurs, ses flags « regardé » et ses babioles, atteignait la limite de 20 000 états après 54 secondes sans finir.

Le reste sort de l'état et des actions essayées : un flag que seul son poseur lit (un marqueur « regardé »), une babiole qu'aucune porte n'exige, une horloge que personne ne lit, un promeneur que personne n'attend, une chaîne de sujets qui finit dans un flag que rien n'utilise.
**Les chapitres** (`checkpoints` avec `goals`, `npm run solve -- --chapters`) : chaque chapitre est prouvé depuis le checkpoint précédent, avec seulement ses propres choses vivantes.
**Les invariants** pour les bugs « plus jamais », vérifiés sur chaque état exploré.
Une résolution globale d'un jeu de 100 lieux et 5 joueurs en six secondes ne promet pas que chaque jeu de 15 heures sera prouvé d'un coup.

rows.heading: Quand ça devient lent : le profil
rows.reason: split across several pages of the catalogue

limits.text: Chaque dimension de l'état (un objet dans le sac, un flag, l'état d'un accessoire, la position d'un script…) est notée par le nombre d'états qui fusionneraient si on la retirait : le haut de cette liste, c'est de quoi la logique du jeu est faite, ou le puzzle devenu combinatoire.

rows.heading: Moins d'ordres : la réduction d'ordre partiel (historique, v2.3)

limits.text: **Ne jamais utiliser la réduction d'ordre partiel pour certifier qu'un jeu n'a pas de softlock.** Mesurée en mode
preuve en 3.3, elle a signalé un softlock qui n'existe pas ([plus bas](#après-v33-noop-memo--pas-de-réduction-dordre-partiel-dans-les-preuves-une-mémoire-des-no-ops-à-la-place)).
`--por` ne s'applique qu'aux recherches de témoin : en mode preuve, le solveur l'ignore et le dit.

Le solveur fusionne déjà les états (un hash) ; ce qu'il payait encore, ce sont les ordres entre les deux : k ramassages indépendants avant une porte font 2^k états quand la recherche ne peut pas finir (la preuve d'une impasse, une recherche tronquée).

`npm run solve -- --por=sleep|stubborn` (`src/engine/tools/por.ts`) utilise ce que le moteur a noté pendant chaque action (ce qu'elle a lu, ce qu'elle a changé, dans les dimensions de l'état) et, pour les actions qu'une condition retient encore, ce que le graphe de puzzles dit qu'elles exigent :
| `tests/fixtures/por.ts`, k ramassages puis une porte qui ne peut pas s'ouvrir | états | exécutions du moteur |

`sleep` ne saute que des exécutions du moteur (une action essayée avant une action indépendante n'est pas réessayée au retour) ; `stubborn` n'explore qu'une action commutante à la fois, donc les états tombent aussi.

rows.heading: v3.1 : schéma 3 et preuve exhaustive (4 octobre 2026)

limits.text: Le témoin n'a pas bougé entre v2.3 et v3.1 (mêmes états, mêmes exécutions : les ids stables ne changent rien à la recherche).

La preuve exhaustive, c'est autre chose : elle visite chaque état atteignable, la réduction d'ordre partiel est coupée dans ce mode (une réduction ne doit pas retirer une branche perdante d'une preuve tant qu'elle n'a pas sa propre preuve d'équivalence), et un jeu de 40 lieux dépasse déjà un budget de 50 000 états.

rows.heading: v3.2 : causes des softlocks, preuve par chapitres, et où la preuve s'arrête (4 octobre 2026)

limits.text: Une preuve rapporte désormais **chaque** état de softlock atteignable (`softlockCount`), regroupés par l'étape qui a perdu la partie (`softlockCauses` : la première action qui mène d'un état encore gagnable à un état qui ne l'est plus), et une preuve depuis « Nouvelle partie » explore aussi les choix de l'introduction (la preuve de la démo passe de 2 176 à 6 528 états : elle n'avait prouvé que la réponse par défaut).
Un seul budget d'états couvre toute la preuve (`maxStates × 10`, au plus 1 000 départs par chapitre) : au-delà, le résultat est `truncated`, jamais vert.

**C'est une limite de la recherche explicite telle qu'elle est écrite, pas du moteur** : l'état garde le lieu exact de chaque personnage et le personnage actif, et un changement de personnage est une transition à part entière, si bien que des états équivalents sont explorés des milliers de fois (trois personnages libres dans 30 lieux : 81 000 combinaisons de positions avant le moindre flag).

Les prochains pas du solveur, dans l'ordre (une relecture extérieure, LOG #38) : mesurer où part le temps (exécutions du moteur, clones, hachages, file) ; une frontière de preuve sans ordre best-first ni chemins copiés ; le personnage actif hors de l'état (les actions de chaque personnage proposées depuis un état canonique, un changement gardé explicite seulement s'il a un effet) ; les **régions de mobilité** (les lieux reliés par des sorties réversibles et silencieuses fusionnés en une région par personnage, les déplacements en macro-étapes dont le trajet est gardé pour la solution) ; des interfaces de chapitre projetées sur ce que la suite lit ; une réduction sûre pour la preuve (fermeture par dépendance, visibilité des objectifs et invariants, blocages, condition de cycle, puisque la propriété est « depuis tout état atteignable la fin reste atteignable »), validée contre la recherche explicite sur des milliers de jeux générés, chaque contre-exemple rejoué sur le vrai moteur ; puis des frontières en parallèle.

rows.heading: v3.3 « Scale » : la matrice de référence (4 octobre 2026)
Après v33-proof-core (exact : mêmes témoins, mêmes preuves, même sortie imprimée sur la démo)

limits.text: Le nombre d'états ne bouge pas, comme il se doit : restent le moteur (environ la moitié), les copies d'état (environ 30 %), et surtout le nombre d'états, auquel s'attaquent les branches suivantes.

rows.heading: Après v33-player-canonical (mêmes verdicts, vérifiés contre la recherche explicite)

limits.text: En mode preuve, des états qui ne diffèrent que par le personnage actif sont un seul état, et chaque état propose les actions de chaque personnage (`Switch to X › action`) quand le changement ne modifie rien de ce que lit le solveur ; un changement qui modifie quelque chose reste une étape explicite, et les invariants sont vérifiés du point de vue de chaque personnage.

rows.heading: Après v33-mobility : régions de mobilité, et la preuve de référence

limits.text: Le lieu exact d'un personnage est remplacé par sa **région** : les lieux entre lesquels il peut marcher en silence (sorties générées et voyages par la carte vers des lieux sans `onEnter`, dont rien ne lit le `visited`, et qu'aucune condition ne nomme), la partie fortement connexe autour de lui vue avec son propre sac.

La preuve propose les actions de chaque lieu de la région sous la forme `Go to <lieu> › action` ; le trajet est joué une fois par lieu, chaque pas vérifié (il arrive, il ne change rien de ce que lit le solveur), et un pas qui n'est pas silencieux relance la recherche avec les lieux exacts (`profile.mobility.reason`).

rows.heading: Après v33-chapter-interfaces : une recherche par chapitre, depuis tous les états frontière à la fois
Après v33-noop-memo : pas de réduction d'ordre partiel dans les preuves, une mémoire des no-ops à la place

limits.text: **La réduction, mesurée en mode preuve.** Les ensembles de sommeil visitent tous les états mais sautent des arêtes : une action déjà essayée dans un ordre qui commute n'est pas relancée.

Sur le jeu par époques, c'est le cas : 20 lieux × 3 personnages signale un softlock que la preuve simple n'a pas (40 × 3 aussi), pour moins de 2 % des exécutions du moteur évitées et 20 à 25 % de temps en plus (`tests/por.test.ts`, « why proof mode keeps the reductions off »).
Une exécution qui n'écrit rien de ce que le solveur hache est gardée avec les valeurs qu'elle a lues ; la même action sur un état aux mêmes valeurs est un no-op aussi, et n'est pas lancée.
Elle suppose que la trace des lectures est complète : un saut sur 16 est lancé quand même et comparé, et une différence est une erreur, jamais un saut silencieux.

rows.heading: 3.3.0, mesurée sur la release (5 octobre 2026, cache coupé)

limits.text: Il échoue (sortie 1) sur toute différence de verdict, d'invariants cassés, d'existence de softlocks, ou de flags, lieux et emplacements atteints ; il dit `partial` (sortie 2) quand la recherche explicite ne tient pas dans le budget, parce qu'alors les verdicts n'ont pas été comparés.

`tests/audit.test.ts` lance le même audit sur 120 jeux aléatoires (`tests/gen/random-game.ts` : 2 à 4 lieux, 1 ou 2 personnages, `has` négatif, consommation, transferts, compteurs, `once` / `nth` / `cycle`, `if` imbriqués), et sur un jeu par commande et par condition du DSL (les deux tables sont vérifiées contre les types `Cmd` et `Cond` : une nouvelle variante sans exemple ne compile pas).
**Un flag mort qui ne l'était pas.** La première règle écrite qui correspond répond.
Un flag qui ne garde qu'une règle antérieure, laquelle ne touche que ce flag, semblait mort à l'analyse de vivacité ; pourtant il décide si c'est la règle antérieure ou une suivante qui répond.

Le solveur fusionnait les deux états et perdait tout chemin passant par la règle suivante ; sur un jeu aléatoire, les abstractions atteignaient par hasard un flag que la recherche explicite n'atteignait pas.
**Lieux atteints.** Avec le personnage canonique, un lieu où seul un autre personnage jouable se tenait manquait à `roomsReached` (et le lint pouvait donc le dire jamais atteint).

rows.heading: 3.4.0, mesurée sur la release (5 octobre 2026, cache coupé)

limits.text: Le résultat dépend donc du lot et jamais du nombre de workers ; un seul worker, c'est la même recherche par lots dans le fil de la recherche.

Un worker qui ne démarre pas, ou s'arrête, laisse ses nœuds au fil de la recherche (le résultat ne change pas ; `profile.workers.reason` le dit) ; les commandes sur mesure arrivent aux workers par le module du jeu ; la réduction d'ordre partiel les tient éteints.

Ce qui ne passe pas à l'échelle : la fusion (les états passent d'un fil à l'autre, le fil de la recherche vérifie chacun), et le démarrage des workers (environ 0,3 s) : une petite preuve, comme chacun des chapitres du jeu d'exemple, n'est pas plus rapide.
Avec plusieurs personnages jouables, lequel porte un objet multiplie les états : trois personnages et douze objets qui circulent librement, c'est la matrice ouverte que la 3.3 ne prouvait pas.

Un objet qu'aucune condition ne lit (son absence ne décide donc de rien : pas de `else`, pas de règle masquée par une qui l'exige), dans aucun invariant ni but, perdu ou déplacé seulement par une action sur lui, et donné par aucune règle ni réaction par type (`poolableItems`), est mis en commun tant que deux personnages quelconques peuvent se rejoindre : l'état garde combien de chaque objet commun existent, pas qui les porte.
Un pas qui ne le fait pas relance la preuve sans mise en commun (`profile.ownership.reason`), comme la mobilité.
L'objectif de la 3.5, la matrice ouverte 20 × 3 dans le budget, **n'est pas atteint**.

Le propriétaire ne s'applique que tant que deux personnages quelconques peuvent se rejoindre, et dans la chaîne ouverte des portes fermées les séparent la plupart du temps (1 817 remises sur 200 000 états).
Comme décidé, cela ne bloque pas la 3.5 ; c'est la question ouverte pour la suite.
**La dominance pour un témoin** (`--dominance`, témoins seulement : elle ne peut élaguer une preuve).
Un état qui n'a pas plus de progrès qu'un état déjà vu (tout le reste égal ; ses objets et flags booléens monotones, ceux dont rien ne lit l'absence, un sous-ensemble) n'est pas exploré.
Une recherche de témoin qui ne trouve rien avec elle est relancée sans, elle ne rend donc jamais `unsolved` d'elle-même.

La recherche « le meilleur d'abord » atteint un témoin avant qu'un état dominé ne sorte, et un état dominé ne sort qu'une fois les meilleurs épuisés, ce qui (quand l'absence n'est jamais lue) veut dire que la recherche échoue de toute façon.
